entry.title: Metabolomics Data and AI Meetings at EMBL-EBI, Hinxton

link.title: Metabolomics Data and AI Meetings at EMBL-EBI, Hinxton

entry.content:
Last week clearly demonstrated EMBL-EBI’s coordinating power in biological data, with three back-to-back events relevant to metabolomics, hosted on campus.

Firstly, visitor Janna Hastings (Idiap Research Institute) gave a fascinating seminar on grounding AI approaches with bio-ontologies, and presented her group’s work on chemical language models and deep learning for classification of chemicals within the ChEBI ontology (Glauer et al. 2024).

Secondly, the MetaboLights team (credit to Noemi Tejera & Thomas Payne for organising) hosted the ELIXIR Metabolomics Community’s face-to-face meeting, followed by the AIBIO-UK x MetaboLights workshop, with diverse attendance from across bioinformatics domains.

During the ELIXIR meeting, I presented an update on my work with the Proteomics Standards Initiative, to expand the Mass Spectrometry Controlled Vocabulary (PSI-MS-CV), in support of cross-repository mapping in the MetabolomicsHub. I then led a discussion on how we can build upon our recent addition to the PSI-MS-CV of chromatographic columns from the RepoRT column database to improve the typically insufficient reporting of chromatographic methods in metabolomics.

Then, during the AIBIO-UK x MetaboLights meeting, I presented a brief overview of our thinking regarding AI integrations for the MetaboLights repository, to seed discussion in the following open session (slides below).

In my opinion, the quality of research presented and discussion was outstanding — due to this abundance I will avoid citing specific cases here as I couldn’t possibly give a sensible overview.

I am writing here with some reflections across a very stimulating (and exhausting) week, in an attempt to draw out some of the overarching themes:

AI-assisted submission: extraction, modelling and mapping

Every repository lives with a tension between rich, standardised metadata and quick, low-effort submission. AI offers a means to bridge this gap whilst improving reporting standards further.

AI proposes, rules verify, people decide. Three sub-tasks to note:

  1. Extraction. Draft metadata from what the submitter already has: the manuscript, acquisition sequences, processing files and raw data. Deterministic readers come first.
  2. Representation. Place each value in the right field of the data model, and validate with deterministic tools. Every field should record whether a person, a parser or a model produced it.
  3. Ontology mapping. Language-model extractors with ontologies as context, map or shortlist terms for the formal description of metadata.

There are encouraging precedents. For example, the community SDRF annotation repository for ProteomeXchange datasets now holds AI-assisted annotations for more than 8,000 datasets from 18 human contributors, built with the agentic sdrf-skills toolkit.

Ontologies and knowledge graphs as ground truth for AI

As Janna argued, generative models are flexible but unreliable. Ontologies support reliable, reproducible inference based on community consensus, but they are brittle, incomplete, shaped by historical choices about scope and persistently under-funded. Knowledge alignment may combine the two so that each covers the other’s weakness.

Questions I am leaving with

None of these is new, but the turn towards AI makes each more urgent.

  1. Vendors. How can the PSI engage instrument vendors early enough to shape implementations? Would a dedicated vendor-liaison group help?
  2. FAIR at source. How do we capture metadata where data are created, chromatographic methods included, instead of reconstructing it at deposition?
  3. Grand challenges. What questions should metabolomics organise around, and how do they become well-posed AI tasks with benchmarks?
  4. Ground truth. How do we make ontologies and knowledge graphs fit to ground AI, with logical axioms rather than bare labels, and with a putative annotation kept distinct from a confirmed identification?
  5. Submission. Can AI make deposition easier without lowering its quality, and can we reinvest the saved effort in richer metadata?
  6. Agent access. How do we open repository data to AI agents whilst preventing excessive bot traffic, maintaining the sustainability of the repository, and ensuring the authors are cited when their data are consumed in bulk?
  7. Annotation evidence. How do we record the chain from spectrum to identity, using mzTab-M and the identifier guidelines of Hajjar et al.?
  8. Sustainability. Who maintains the ontologies that AI will rely on? Ontology development is consensus creation, and consensus does not automate.

What next

Several of these threads continue at the de.NBI & ELIXIR-DE BioHackathon Germany in Göttingen on 7–11 December, the EuBIC-MS hackathon in Gimo, Sweden, on 31 January–5 February 2027, and the HUPO-PSI Spring Meeting in Antwerp on 6–9 April 2027.

The MetaboLights team and I are actively pursuing the development of AI integrations, including a submission workflow.

If you are working on any of these questions, or think I have framed one wrongly, I would love to hear from you.
entry.summary: Reflections on a week of metabolomics data and AI meetings at EMBL-EBI, and the questions I am leaving with.

entry.title: MetaboLights and AIBIO-UK workshop
entry.content:
Reproduced from the original LinkedIn post.

Come visit EBI and join the discussion on the use of AI to further the metabolomics field.

Personally, I’ll be looking to learn and contribute in some current areas of interest, including:

  • Automated dataset metadata annotation, either at submission or during retrospective curation.
  • The role of semantics, ontologies/controlled vocabularies, and knowledge graphs in enabling accurate AI accelerated metabolomics.
  • The intersection between AI and chemistry, specifically effective chemical structure and name handling.
  • Current methods in molecular/spectral networking, parameterless peak-picking, and in silico spectral prediction.

This is a timely and well-targeted workshop, co-located with the ELIXIR metabolomics community meeting. I anticipate a highly productive meeting driven by a critical mass of scientists, developers, informaticians and more, bringing experiences from a cross-section of scientific domains. Registration is open (link below) - I hope to see you there!

Thomas Payne · reposted

🚀 Particularly excited about this one…

What will it take to unlock the potential of public data to power AI at scale in metabolomics?

On Friday 23 October, #MetaboLights and #AIBIOUK will bring the metabolomics and AI communities together at European Bioinformatics Institute EMBL-EBI, Hinxton, UK, to explore exactly that.

🧠 AI + metabolomics: real-world use cases
🌐 Public data: opportunities, barriers and priorities
🔗 AI-ready data: context, semantics and provenance
💡 Working together: connect, share and shape

Whether your work spans #Metabolomics, #AI or beyond - academia or industry - we would love to have you join us and help build what comes next. 🚀

👉 Registration is now open: https://lnkd.in/e4W5uM7C

The workshop is co-located with the ELIXIR Metabolomics Community Meeting (21-22 October).

entry.title: HUPO-PSI Spring Meeting, Rome
entry.content:
Last week, I attended the HUPO-PSI Spring Workshop at the National Research Council of Italy (CNR) in Rome.

It was a pleasure to meet colleagues including Eric Deutsch and Joshua Klein that I have worked with extensively online through my contributions to the PSI-MS Controlled Vocabulary.

The main auditorium, Sala Marconi, had a striking wrap-around mural reflecting Italian science. To me, this evoked thoughts of the Scientific Revolution and Age of Enlightenment and was an inspiring environment for discussion.

Another key focus, personally, were the mzTab-M working group sessions, led by Nils Hoffmann & Philippine Louail. mzTab-M is an open data standard for the sharing of mass spectrometric metabolimics results, with much potential to streamline the data processing to open data repository workflow for researchers. I hope to continue to become more familiar with mzTab-M and contribute to this project in the future, alongside my EMBL-EBI Metabolomics colleague Ozgur Yurekten, who is already involved.

I gave a presentation in the ‘Metabolomics Education’ session, giving a brief introduction on MetaboLights study content and submission - rooted in the underlying ISA-Tab data model. This served as a prelude to Ozgur’s hands-on workshop on ‘mzTab-M to ISA-Tab to MetaboLights’ study submission.

I also presented the below four page digital poster on the MetabolomicsHub, and was encouraged by the interest and discussion from the other attendees.

Last but not least, I snuck off Wednesday night to have a gentle run around Rome exploring many of the tourist hotspots:
